strengths: Novel theoretical analysis: Theorem 1 rigorously establishes DDPO-DSM equivalence, providing fundamental insight into what DDPO optimizes
Rigorous variance analysis: Theorem 2 formally quantifies variance increase from noisy conditioning with explicit κ(s,t) formula; proofs are sound and well-structured
Strong empirical validation of theory: Controlled CIFAR-10/ImageNet-64 experiments (Figure 3) directly demonstrate that noisy-DSM converges slower, validating Theorem 2
Substantial practical speedups: Consistent 8-24× improvements across multiple metrics (GenEval, OCR, PickScore) and models (SD3.5M, FLUX) without quality degradation
Conceptual unification: Elegantly aligns diffusion RL with LLM RL—both optimize same objective with reward-dependent weighting, removing step-wise likelihood dependency
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with effective schematic figures, consistent notation, detailed pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and clear mathematical exposition
Comprehensive empirical analysis: Ablations on timestep sampling, KL strength, and on-policy vs. off-policy; qualitative examples showing improvements
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: Only compared to Flow-GRPO; missing comparisons to original DDPO, DanceGRPO, TempFlow, and other reward-weighted approaches reduces confidence in claimed superiority

Ad-hoc design choice: Using w(t)=1 instead of standard ELBO weighting w(t) is justified only empirically, with vague explanation about 'visual quality vs. likelihood'; disconnects from the ELBO-based theoretical framework

Unquantified discretization error: Theorem 1 holds 'up to discretization error' but paper doesn't analyze magnitude. Flow-GRPO baseline uses plain Euler-Maruyama (which increases variance per footnote 2), leaving gap between theory and practice

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported despite G=24 batch size. Variance of key metrics (convergence time, GenEval scores) should be quantified to assess stability of 8-24× speedup claims

No variance measurements on main tasks: While Theorem 2 is rigorously proven, direct empirical measurement of AWM's variance reduction on RL tasks is absent. Figure 3 validates on pretraining but not on actual reward optimization
Limited scope of validation: No video generation experiments despite mentioning its importance; unclear if method generalizes beyond image generation to other domains

Incomplete reproducibility: Code link missing in abstract; reward function implementations (GenEval, OCR) not described; exact sampling/evaluation procedures and computational requirements not specified

Single benefit dimension: GenEval shows identical quality (0.95 vs 0.95); improvements on OCR/PickScore also show same performance with just faster convergence. Discussion of whether quality improvements are achievable would strengthen motivation

Underexplored design flexibility: While claiming AWM 'supports any sampler/noise level,' only Euler-Maruyama tested. Advanced ODE solvers and different noise schedules not evaluated despite being presented as advantages

Speedup attribution unclear: No decomposition of 8-24× speedup into components (variance reduction vs. training timestep reduction vs. other factors), making it difficult to attribute improvements to specific mechanisms

strengths: Sound theoretical analysis establishing connection between DDPO and denoising score matching with noisy conditioning (Theorem 1); elegant variance decomposition (Theorem 2) with rigorous proofs
Empirical validation of theoretical predictions via CIFAR-10/ImageNet-64 pretraining experiments showing noisy-DSM converges slower than clean-DSM
Substantial practical speedups (8-24×) on multiple benchmarks and large-scale models (SD3.5M, FLUX)
Clear presentation with intuitive figures, algorithmic clarity, and reasonable ablation studies on timestep sampling and KL regularization
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: AWM is a straightforward application of the theoretical insight (advantage-weighted score matching). Concurrent work (FMPG, Fan et al. 2025) pursues similar approaches, with unclear differentiation

Discretization error inadequately addressed: Theorem 1 proof states 'omitting discretization error' without quantifying its magnitude; assumes approximation holds at practical timesteps where Δt is non-negligible

Experimental rigor concerns: (1) No error bars or multiple runs reported; (2) Single training runs compared make speedup claims unreliable; (3) Hardware/implementation parity with Flow-GRPO baseline unclear; (4) No human evaluation of quality

Hyperparameter sensitivity contradicts 'simplicity' claims: KL strength β requires careful tuning (Figure 7b shows instability at β=0.2, collapse at β=2.0); uniform time weighting w(t)=1 departs from principled ELBO weighting, weakening theoretical justification

Theory-practice gap: Theory emphasizes variance reduction, but empirical results emphasize wall-clock speedup. No direct variance measurements during RL training to confirm mechanism; 8-24× speedups are much larger than modest slowdowns shown in Figure 3 for small-scale pretraining

Limited experimental scope: Only text-to-image generation tested; only recent models (SD3.5M, FLUX); only smooth reward functions (GenEval, OCR, PickScore); scalability to other modalities, binary rewards, or multiple objectives unstudied

Quality improvements marginal or absent: GenEval 0.95 vs. 0.95 (identical); PickScore on SD3.5M 23.25 vs. 23.01 (<1% gain); claims 'without compromising quality' but quality not improved, only efficiency gained

Missing critical implementation details: Fixed 4 training timesteps without sensitivity analysis; decoupling of training/sampling timesteps mentioned as advantage but never experimentally demonstrated; LoRA ranks chosen without justification; group-relative advantage sensitivity to G=24 not studied

Overclaimed conceptual contributions: Analogy to LLM pretraining+RL overstated; diffusion score matching with weights is conceptually different from LLM likelihood optimization despite superficial parallels
Code reproducibility: URL placeholder missing; some hyperparameter choices lack justification (e.g., LoRA configuration, learning rate schedule)

strengths: Clear theoretical contribution establishing DDPO as implicit DSM with noisy conditioning (Theorem 1), with rigorous variance quantification (Theorem 2) showing noisy targets increase variance
Substantial and well-validated practical speedups (8.02× GenEval, 23.6× OCR, 10.5× PickScore) across multiple state-of-the-art models (SD3.5M, FLUX) without quality degradation
Excellent presentation with intuitive figures and clear progression from diagnosis to solution; Algorithm 1 and ablations support reproducibility
Conceptual unification of diffusion and LLM RL, both optimizing pretraining objectives with reward-dependent weighting
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple metrics and models with supporting visual results and honest treatment of discretization error limitations
weaknesses: Limited novelty: once noisy DSM conditioning is diagnosed, applying advantage-weighted clean DSM is a natural solution combining well-established RL techniques
Theory-practice gap: variance analysis proven on small datasets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-64) using EDM, not directly validated on large text-to-image models where speedups are claimed

Critical design choices under-justified: uniform weight w(t)=1 deviates from ELBO without ablation; KL strength varies drastically across tasks (β∈[0.4,1.0] vs 0.01); dependence on 4 training timesteps not thoroughly explored
Incomplete method comparison: only Flow-GRPO baseline tested despite citing DanceGRPO, TempFlow, MixGRPO, and BranchGRPO as related work

Generalization limitations: only LoRA training tested; sampler flexibility claimed as advantage but not experimentally validated; tested on only 2 models; on-policy vs off-policy (Fig 7c) shows negligible difference contradicting variance-reduction narrative

strengths: Novel theoretical insight establishing that DDPO implicitly performs DSM with noisy targets, providing new understanding of the objective mismatch between pretraining and RL post-training
Rigorous mathematical analysis with formal variance characterization (Theorem 2.3) showing κ(s,t) additional conditional covariance, supported by detailed proofs
Empirical validation of theoretical predictions through pretraining experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64 (Figure 3, Table 6) directly confirming variance predictions
Substantial practical speedups demonstrated consistently across multiple models (SD3.5M, FLUX) and metrics (GenEval 16.54×, OCR 19.13×, PickScore 34.67×) without quality degradation
Simple and generalizable method decoupled from sampler choice, enabling use with any ODE/SDE solver while maintaining alignment with pretraining objective
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including detailed ablation studies (Figures 7-8), multiple benchmarks, and reproducibility details (Algorithm 1, detailed hyperparameters in appendix)
Clear presentation with effective figures and mathematical exposition; code availability promised
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis operates at oracle level assuming population-level objectives and omitting Euler-Maruyama discretization error, which the paper acknowledges is 'inherent to DDPO formulation', creating gap between theory and practical discretized algorithms

Limited baseline comparisons—only evaluated against Flow-GRPO and TempFlow-GRPO, missing comparisons to DanceGRPO, other recent GRPO variants, and continuous-time RL approaches mentioned in related work
Lack of statistical significance testing with no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; unclear whether improvements like PickScore (23.01→23.11) are statistically significant

Speedup attribution unclear due to multiple confounding factors: different samplers (SA-Solver vs. unspecified baseline), different hyperparameters (w(t), timesteps, guidance scale, β, reference model), and different experimental configurations between early and later experiments

Extended training required for best quality: Table 2 shows AWM† needs 58 GPU hours for OCR 0.96 (vs. 21.76 hours for 0.92), somewhat undermining the '16.54× speedup' claim when comparing to best achievable quality

Missing critical ablations: no ablation of advantage weighting alone, no comparison of standard DSM with advantage weighting, no systematic study of w(t) impact despite switching between configurations

Variance analysis conditional on fixed xt; formal connection between reduced conditional variance and improved full optimization trajectory not established, relying on empirical validation rather than theoretical convergence guarantees

strengths: Novel theoretical insight: Theorem 2.1 establishes the equivalence between DDPO and noisy-target DSM, providing genuine understanding of existing methods
Rigorous variance analysis: Theorem 2.3 formally quantifies how noisy targets increase conditional covariance, with explicit κ(s,t) bounds and empirical validation
Strong empirical results: Consistent speedups (16-34×) across multiple models (SD3.5M, FLUX) and metrics (GenEval, OCR, PickScore) with maintained/improved quality
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple ablations, diverse benchmarks, sampler flexibility validation, and direct variance measurement (Table 6)
Conceptual elegance: Unifying pretraining and RL under the same matching objective mirrors the LLM paradigm
weaknesses: Critical gap between theory and practice: Theorems assume oracle/population-level objectives while omitting discretization error, which could be the actual source of DDPO slowness. Causality between noisy-target variance and convergence slowness not rigorously established

Confounded experimental comparison: AWM uses SA-Solver (different hyperparameters, noise level, guidance, MC samples) than Flow-GRPO. Unclear whether speedups come from the algorithm or tuning. Flow-GRPO hyperparameters not reported as tuned equivalently

Limited methodological novelty: AWM is straightforward advantage-weighted score matching. While theoretically motivated, the algorithmic contribution is incremental. Concurrent FMPG work proposes nearly identical approach

Unanalyzed ELBO approximation: Using ELBO instead of true likelihood (Eq. 15) introduces additional approximation error not quantified in theory or experiments. Double approximation (policy likelihood + loss) not justified

No convergence guarantees: AWM lacks convergence rate analysis. How does advantage weighting affect convergence? What is the policy-gradient variance? Missing sample complexity bounds relating variance increase to iteration complexity
Incomplete variance analysis: Table 6 measures target variance but this is only one component. No empirical comparison of actual gradient variance during AWM vs DDPO training on same setup
Theoretical gaps in KL term: KL regularization (Eq. 16) uses velocity MSE similar to DDPO. Why isn't this noisy-target DSM? Ablations show stability dependence but no theoretical analysis

Limited baselines and scope: Only Flow-GRPO and TempFlow-GRPO compared. No comparison with concurrent methods (FMPG, Zhao et al. 2025). Experiments limited to image generation; video/other modalities largely absent
Overstated claims: Mode decoupling overstated (requires specific samplers), quality preservation claim needs qualification (modest improvements on some metrics). 'No CFG in training' not unique

Presentation issues: Inconsistent notation, insufficient discussion of theory-practice disconnect, informal Algorithm 1 pseudocode, limited reproducibility details (code not released, different early/late configurations)

strengths: Novel theoretical insight showing DDPO implicitly performs DSM with noisy targets (Theorem 2.1), rigorously proven and validated empirically
Comprehensive variance analysis (Theorem 2.3) explicitly quantifying the cost of noisy targets, with direct empirical measurement confirming predictions
Strong experimental results demonstrating up to 34× speedup over Flow-GRPO across multiple models (SD3.5M, FLUX) and metrics (GenEval, OCR, PickScore) while maintaining or improving quality
Elegant conceptual contribution unifying pretraining and RL in diffusion models under a common score/flow matching objective with reward-dependent weighting
Thorough experimental validation including CIFAR-10/ImageNet-64 pretraining studies, comprehensive ablations, ODE/SDE compatibility tests, and mode coverage analysis
Technical flexibility: decouples training from sampling, supports any ODE/SDE sampler, and avoids CFG requirement during training
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-4) and complete mathematical derivations in appendices
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: analysis operates at population level (ignoring discretization error), uses exact objectives while practice employs ELBO surrogates (Eq. 14), and local gradient relation (Eq. 10) derived only at frozen policy—actual training dynamics not covered

Two significantly different experimental configurations (early vs later with different w(t), samplers, Monte Carlo steps, and β values) create confusion; main results use later config showing 16.54× speedup but early config shows only 8.02×, suggesting configuration sensitivity

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Flow-GRPO is primary baseline but direct DDPO comparison absent; TempFlow-GRPO only shown for GenEval; concurrent related methods (Lee et al. 2023, Fan et al. 2025, McAllister et al. 2025) not experimentally compared
Unexplained variance in speedup across metrics: PickScore shows 34.67× vs GenEval 16.54× on SD3.5M, and 6.82× vs 8.53× on FLUX—root causes of metric-specific differences not analyzed

Limited sensitivity analysis: group size G=24 not ablated, KL coefficient β appears task-dependent (0.01-0.4 in early config) without systematic study, no analysis of which reward types or task properties favor AWM
Narrow experimental scope: only text-to-image generation tested; no video, 3D, or other modalities; only large foundation models (SD3.5M, FLUX); scalability to smaller models unclear
Missing theoretical justification for practical choices: importance sampling ratio (Eq. 15), time-weighting w(t)=t vs w(t)=1, and GRPO framework with KL regularization lack theoretical grounding

Reproducibility limitations: requires proprietary models and third-party reward functions (GenPT-4o for GenEval); two configurations create uncertainty about which settings to adopt; hyperparameters appear task-tuned
